galeria.copy: The director of MIT’s fusion center — the man closest to giving the world unlimited clean energy — was shot six times in his apartment lobby in December. No robbery. No motive. Six months later gas is $4.50 a gallon, the Strait of Hormuz is closed, refineries are exploding across four continents, and eleven scientists with nuclear clearances are dead or missing. My brother is the FBI investigator who’s been working these cases. Last month he connected something across all of them that made his supervisors shut him down mid-sentence. That night he pulled his kids out of school, moved his family ninety miles from anything, and called me at 11 PM. What he told me in that diner I can’t keep to myself anymore. His name is Danny. Seventeen years at the bureau. The guy they pull in when cases don’t make sense — when three investigations in three states start rhyming and nobody can figure out why. His thing is patterns. Always has been. He sees the thread between cases other agents file separately and forget about. Cold cases that turn out not to be cold. Missing persons that turn out not to be random. He’s the one in the room who says pull up the other file and everyone’s stomach drops because he’s always right. In seventeen years he has never talked about work. Not once. Not a name. Not a case. Not even a bad day. My wife used to ask him what he does at Thanksgiving and he’d smile and say “paperwork.” Every year. Same answer. Same smile. She stopped asking about five years ago. I’m his younger brother. I sell insurance. I have a wife — Sarah — and two kids. Caleb is 9. Emma is 6. We live in a suburb outside Charlotte. Normal life. Normal street. The kind of neighborhood where the biggest problem is someone’s recycling bin blowing into the road. Danny and I aren’t distant. We’re just different. I call him on his birthday. He texts back a day late. We see each other at Christmas. He brings good whiskey and never stays past ten. Which is why when his name showed up on my phone at 11:14 on a Tuesday night, I sat up in bed before I even answered. “I need you to come see me this weekend.” “What’s wrong?” “Nothing’s wrong. Don’t bring Sarah. Just come alone.” “Danny.” “I can’t do this on the phone. Saturday morning. I’ll text you a location.” He hung up. My wife rolled over. “Who was that?” “Danny.” “Is he okay?” I didn’t answer because I didn’t know. Saturday. 7 AM. I drove three hours south to a diner off a state highway I’d never been on. Danny picked the spot. Texted me mile markers instead of an address. Said don’t use GPS. Delete the texts when you get here. When I walked in, he was in the last booth in the back. Facing the door. No phone on the table. Bag under his seat. Coffee untouched. He looked like a different person. Unshaved. Eyes hollow. A jacket I’d never seen — no logo, no markings, nothing on it. He didn’t stand up. Didn’t smile. “Sit down.” I sat down. “You didn’t tell Sarah?” “No.” “Good.” He stared at his coffee for a while. Then he looked up at me. “I’m going to tell you something I’ve never told anyone outside of work. And when I’m done you’re going to want me to say I’m exaggerating. I won’t be.” “Okay.” “You’ve seen the news about the scientists?” “The missing ones? Yeah. Everyone’s seen that.” “It’s not just missing. Some of them are dead. Shot. Close range. No robbery. No motive that holds up.” “Okay.” “The director of MIT’s fusion center. Portuguese. Forty-seven years old. Six shell casings in his apartment lobby back in December. This man was running the most advanced clean energy research in the country. Plasma physics. Fusion. The kind of work that — if it succeeds — makes oil worthless. Makes refineries worthless. Makes the entire energy grid as we know it worthless. He was close. Closer than anyone. And then he was dead.” “Jesus.” “A Caltech astrophysicist. Shot on his front porch. February. A retired Air Force general who ran the research lab at Wright-Patterson — vanished from Albuquerque with a revolver and no phone. A DOE contractor from a nuclear weapons facility — walked out of his house and never came back. Two Los Alamos workers — gone. A NASA JPL engineer — gone. Phones left behind. Factory-reset. Wiped clean.” “Danny.” “Eleven. Eleven people with the highest clearances this country issues. Dead or gone. In two years.” “Trump said they’re looking into it.” “They are. And I’ve been looking into it longer than anyone at the White House has.” He took a sip of his cold coffee. “These landed on my desk one at a time. Different field offices. Different states. Massachusetts. California. New Mexico. Connecticut. Each filed as a standalone. Nobody connecting them because they’re spread out. Different causes. Different circumstances.” “But you started connecting them.” “By case four or five my brain was doing what it always does.” “The pattern thing.” “The pattern thing. Same profile. Same clearance level. Same clean exits. The kills are precise — no collateral, no witnesses, no noise. The disappearances are surgical — they leave behind everything that’s trackable and take nothing except what lets them vanish. Or be vanished.” “What are you saying?” “I’m not done.” He leaned forward. “While these people — the ones who could solve the world’s energy problem forever — are being removed from the board, ask yourself what’s happening to the energy that already exists.” “What do you mean?” “The refineries.” “Valero Port Arthur. March 23rd. Explosion so big it shook houses miles away. One of the largest refineries in the country. 400,000 barrels a day.” “I remember that.” “Chevron El Segundo. Jet fuel unit. Marathon Texas City. Then it went global. Geelong, Australia — one of the country’s last working refineries. Romania — a power plant transformer blew and knocked out part of Bucharest’s grid. India — a brand new refinery exploded the day before the prime minister was supposed to cut the ribbon.” “Some of that is the war.” “Some of it is. Some of it isn’t. Eight major incidents. Four continents. Sixty days. That’s an 1800 percent spike above the normal rate.” “Eighteen hundred percent.” “That’s not wear and tear. That’s not deferred maintenance. That’s not bad luck. I’ve been doing this for seventeen years and I’ve never seen a pattern this clean in anything I’ve investigated.” He waited. “Now put those two things next to each other.” “Which two things?” “The scientists. And the refineries.” I didn’t answer. But I felt something shift in my chest. “The people who could build a future beyond oil — removed. The machines that keep the present running on oil — destroyed. Both sides of the energy equation. The future and the present. At the same time. In the same window.” “Danny. Who is doing this?” “That’s the wrong question.” “Then what’s the right question?” “The right question is what comes next.” He reached under the table and pulled a folder out of the bag. “When my supervisors shut me down, I kept pulling on my own time. Off the system. Printed files. My own notes. And I found something.” He slid the folder across the table. “This is a published document. Not classified. Not hidden. Anybody can find it if they know where to look. It’s an energy transition framework. Phases. Timelines. Benchmarks for when specific infrastructure gets taken offline. Targets for when populations shift from open energy access to managed allocation.” “Managed allocation?” “Rationing. They just use cleaner words.” I opened it. Dates. Phases. Charts. “Read the timeline. Then look at my case files.” I looked. The scientists who could break the energy bottleneck — gone. Removed from the board at the exact point the timeline said alternative energy paths needed to be closed off. The refineries keeping everything running right now — burning. Taken offline at the exact point the timeline said fossil fuel capacity needed to be consolidated. Both sides. In sequence. On schedule. “Danny. What is this?” “This is what I wasn’t supposed to find.” “You remember 2020?” “COVID. Yeah.” “The lockdowns. They told you which stores were essential. How far you could drive. How many people you could have in your own living room.” “Yeah.” “That wasn’t a one-time thing.” I felt something cold move through me. “That was a rehearsal. For what’s coming now. Same playbook. Different reason. 2020 was health. This one is energy.” “Energy lockdown.” “That phrase is going to be everywhere within weeks. Watch for it.” “That can’t happen here.” “It’s already happening. Just not here yet.” He started listing. “The Philippines declared a national energy emergency. Moved the whole country to a four-day work week. Sri Lanka made Wednesdays a public holiday — gas capped at less than four gallons a week — their president went on TV and said prepare for the worst. Bangladesh cut work hours and closed shopping centers by 6 PM. People fought each other at gas stations. Egypt dimmed the streetlights and closed restaurants by 9. India ran out of cooking gas. People are burning firewood.” “Those are other countries.” “Those are the small dominoes. They fall first because nobody here pays attention to them. Then the medium ones start cracking — Europe. Australia. Japan. That’s what you’re watching right now. Spirit Airlines isn’t flying anymore. Gone. Seventeen thousand jobs, overnight. Lufthansa slashed 20,000 flights. The head of the international energy agency called this the biggest supply disruption in the history of the oil market. Gas just crossed four fifty a gallon. Groceries jumped the most in four years. Inflation’s at a three-year high.” “Okay.” “By the time the big domino — America — tips, it’s already too late. The shelves are already thin. The gas is already short. The grid is already stressed. And the average person looks up from their phone and goes ‘wait, what happened?’ That person is the last one to know. That person is the one standing in line.” “In line for what?” “For everything. Gas cards. Ration limits. Rolling power schedules. Please reduce usage between 4 and 9 PM. Stay home if your trip isn’t essential. 2020 without the masks. Except this one doesn’t end in three weeks. This one ends when the oil starts moving again. Months. Maybe longer.” I sat there. “Danny. So what do I do?” He looked at his coffee. Looked at the folder. Looked at me. “Everything I just told you — the gas, the flights, the grid, the rations — that’s the part people are going to panic about. That’s the part that’ll be on every channel. Everybody is going to be focused on the energy.” “Yeah.” “Nobody is going to think about the water.” “Water?” “Water.” His voice dropped. “When the grid starts going down — rolling blackouts, brownouts, whatever soft word they use — the water stops. Not eventually. Fast. The pumps that push clean water from the treatment plant to your faucet run on electricity. No power, no pumps. No pumps, no tap.” “In how long?” “Hours.” “Hours?” “Texas. 2021. Three-day grid failure. Weather did it. Not a war. Not a blockade. Just ice. Millions of people lost safe water. Boil advisories for weeks after the power came back.” “Millions?” “From a three-day accident. What we’re looking at isn’t three days. And it isn’t an accident.” He set his coffee down. “Picture it. Your kids are thirsty. The shelves are cleared out. The tap isn’t safe. There’s no delivery truck on the way. And you’re standing in your kitchen trying to figure out what you’re going to give a six-year-old to drink.” I didn’t say anything. “Everybody is going to be fighting over gas and groceries. The person who figured out the water before everyone else — that person is in a different position entirely.” “So what are you doing about it?” “I’ve got it handled.” “What does that mean?” “It means I’ve got it handled. For my kids. For Jen. For my partner and his family.” “Danny.” “This isn’t something I’m spreading around.” “You just told me my daughter might not have drinking water and you’re going to sit there and say you’ve got it handled?” He didn’t say anything for a while. Then he leaned down and unzipped the bag under the booth. Not the laptop bag. The other one. He pulled out something folded and blue. A water bag. A hose. A small filter. A clear pouch tucked inside. He set it on the table between our coffee cups. Not a straw. Not a bottle. A full gravity system. “What is that?” “This is what we’re all using. Every person in my world who understands the water side of this has one. My supervisor — the one who shut me down — had two in his office drawer the same day he told me to stop looking. That’s when I knew for sure.” “Knew what?” “That he believed me.” I looked down at the blue bag. Danny unfolded it slowly. “This is what people miss. A straw helps one person drink. That’s fine if you’re alone. But you have Sarah. Caleb. Emma. Your parents. A family doesn’t need sips. A family needs gallons.” That line hit harder than anything else he’d said. A family needs gallons. He pointed to the top bag. “Dirty freshwater goes here. Creek. pond. lake. river. rainwater. Anything fresh you can safely get to. You hang it up. Gravity pulls the water through the filter. Clean water comes out below into the pouch.” “No power?” “No.” “No batteries?” “No.” “No pumping?” “No.” “Chemicals?” “No.” He looked at me. “That’s the point. If the grid is the problem, your water plan can’t need the grid.” I picked it up. It was lighter than I expected. “This is really what you’re using?” “My house. Jen’s car. My truck. My partner’s house. My parents. My kids know where theirs is.” He tapped the bag. “One gallon at a time. Up to 1,500 gallons depending on source water and maintenance. 0.1-micron filter. The stuff that usually makes natural water dangerous — bacteria, parasites, protozoa, microplastics — that’s what this is for.” “Danny. Does it actually work?” “I’m about to show you. But first — take this.” He pulled a napkin from the dispenser. Took a pen from his jacket. Wrote a web address on it. Folded it in half. Slid it across the table next to my coffee. “Put that in your wallet. When you’re ready, that’s where you go. Small outfit. Guard Survival. These aren’t the kind of thing people think about until they need them. And by the time they need them, they’re already late.” I put the napkin in my wallet. “Now come outside.” We walked out the back of the diner. There was a drainage creek that ran along the tree line past the parking lot. Murky. Brownish-green. Leaves sitting on the surface. Smelled like wet dirt and standing water. The kind of water you tell your kids not to touch. Danny knelt down. Filled the top bag straight from the creek. Water that looked like weak iced tea. Something floating in it I didn’t want to identify. He walked to a low branch near the back of the lot and hung the bag. Connected the hose. Set the clean pouch underneath. Opened the valve. For a few seconds, nothing happened. Then water started moving. Slow at first. Then steady. No pump. No battery. No noise. Just gravity. The dirty water stayed in the top bag. Clear water came through the hose into the clean pouch below. I just stared at it. Danny lifted the pouch. “Smell it.” I did. Nothing. No creek smell. No algae. No mud. He poured some into a bottle. It was clear. Then he drank first. Of course he did. He took a long drink, handed the bottle to me, and said, “Your turn.” I looked at the creek. Looked at the bottle. Looked at my brother. Then I drank. I expected it to taste like the creek looked. It didn’t. It tasted like water. Regular water. Like out of a fridge filter at home. Cold because the creek was cold. No grit. No taste. No anything. I pulled it away and stared at it. “What the hell.” “That’s the whole point.” “From a drainage creek behind a diner.” “From any freshwater source you can safely get to. The creek your kids ride past on the way to school. The retention pond in your neighborhood. The river you drive over on your way to work. Every source of fresh water you’ve been ignoring your whole life — that’s your supply. You just didn’t know it.” I drove home. Three hours. Radio off the whole way. I told myself Danny was burned out. Working too many cases. Seeing patterns where there were none. That’s the risk of his job — eventually you connect things that aren’t connected. I almost convinced myself. Monday morning. Headline. California brownout advisory. Voluntary. Reduce usage between 4 and 9 PM. Tuesday. Another refinery. Chalmette, Louisiana. PBF Energy. Explosion in a reformer unit. Black smoke for miles. Third one this spring. Wednesday. Gas at $4.55 at the station near my house. I watched a woman in a minivan stare at the price on the pump for ten seconds, then put the nozzle back and drive away. Thursday. Grocery prices up the most in four years. Tomatoes up 40 percent. Coffee up almost 20. The news said energy costs were behind all of it. Every single thing Danny told me at that diner was already showing up on my screen. I sat on the couch at midnight. House dark. Sarah asleep. Kids asleep. I pulled the napkin out of my wallet. Typed the address into my phone. Ordered at 12:47 AM. I didn’t order one. I ordered for my whole family. My parents. Sarah’s mother. One for the house. One for the car. One for anyone who would call me if the tap stopped. That Saturday morning I drove to the creek behind Emma’s elementary school. End of our street. I’ve driven past it every single day for six years. My kids throw rocks in it after pickup. I brought the Aqua-GS1 and an empty bottle. The water was greenish-brown. Smelled like wet leaves and algae. I filled the dirty-water bag. Hung it from a branch. Connected the hose. Set the clean pouch underneath. Opened the valve. Same thing. Dirty water in the top. Clear water below. I stood there holding the bottle, looking at a creek I’d ignored for six years. A quarter mile from my front door. Clean water. Right there. The whole time. I told Sarah everything that night. The diner. The cases. The scientists. The refineries. The timeline. The water. She sat on the edge of the bed and listened without saying a word. When I finished, she stood up and walked into the other room. I thought she was angry. I thought she thought I’d finally lost my mind the same way Danny’s girlfriend thought Danny had lost his. Three days went by. She didn’t mention it. Wednesday I came home from work and there was a printed map on the kitchen counter. Every creek, pond, and body of water within five miles of our house. Highlighted. Distances written in her handwriting. Routes drawn. She was at the stove making dinner. Didn’t look up. “I mapped three routes Emma could walk on her own if she had to.” That’s all she said. I don’t know who’s going to read this. I don’t know if you’ve been watching the same things I’ve been watching and feeling the same thing in your stomach that I couldn’t name until Danny named it for me in that diner. But if my brother — a man who has spent seventeen years training himself not to see patterns that aren’t real — is telling me to get ready, I’m getting ready. He said most people will find out what’s coming from the evening news. By then it’s too late. You’re finding out right now. Don’t waste it. This is the same site Danny wrote on that napkin at the diner. https://guardsurvival.com/products/aqua-gs1 The Aqua-GS1 is a one-gallon gravity-fed water filtration system. You fill the top bag from a freshwater source like a creek, pond, lake, river, or rainwater, hang it, and gravity pulls the water through the 0.1-micron filter into the clean pouch below. No power. No batteries. No pumping. No chemicals. Up to 1,500 gallons depending on source water and maintenance. Not saltwater. Not chemical runoff. Be smart about your source. But if there is freshwater nearby, this gives your family a way to make clean water by the gallon. And that is the part most families are not ready for. There is water around you. You just need a way to make it safe. https://guardsurvival.com/products/aqua-gs1 EDITED: Since I posted this three things happened. California’s brownout advisory shifted from voluntary to mandatory in two regions. Danny told me at the diner to watch for that exact language change. He said first it’s voluntary. Then mandatory. Then rolling. Then it stops being temporary. A news anchor on cable used the phrase “energy lockdown” on air. I felt my chest tighten. Danny said that phrase would start showing up within weeks. It took less than two. My brother-in-law — Sarah’s brother, the one who gave me a look when I handed him the link — texted me yesterday. “Hey where did you get that water bag thing? Buddy of mine at the fire station said their whole crew has gravity systems.” That’s the guy who thought I was being dramatic. He’s not calling me dramatic anymore. https://guardsurvival.com/products/aqua-gs1 P.S. — I called Danny last night. First time since the diner. I asked him if anything had changed. He was quiet for a few seconds. Then he said, “It’s moving faster than I thought it would.” I asked what that means. He said, “It means the people I told to get ready have less time than I gave them.” Then he said he loved me. Danny has never said that to me. Not once in my life. I hung up and sat in my truck in the driveway for twenty minutes. I didn’t sleep that night. P.P.S. — The Aqua-GS1 does up to 1,500 gallons depending on source water and maintenance. But he said if you only get one thing first, solve water. You can deal with expensive gas. You can deal with the cold. You can sit in the dark. WARNING: I made a huge mistake after I bought the Complete Ethiopian Bible from FaithMade. I almost threw it away. Don't do what I almost did. Three weeks after I started reading it, I had it back in the box, ready to throw it in the trash. Not because it wasn't working. Because of what started happening after I opened it. Let me explain. I'm 54. I've been a Christian my entire life. Raised in church, never missed a Sunday, the whole thing. And somewhere along the way I had quietly accepted that a certain emptiness was just my normal. The prayers that felt like they hit the ceiling and stopped. The heaviness on my chest I could never explain. Reading scripture and still feeling lost, still feeling like I was on the outside of something everyone else seemed to feel. I'd asked God for answers for years and mostly heard silence. And like most women in my seat, I blamed myself. Figured I wasn't faithful enough. Not good enough. Not chosen the way other people were. Then one night I went down an internet rabbit hole and found out the Bible I'd been reading my whole life was missing twenty-two books. And that one nation had kept all eighty-eight of them for more than seventeen hundred years. That's when I found the Complete Ethiopian Bible from FaithMade. The full canon, eighty-eight books, in English. With the strange-sounding titles I'd never heard in any church I'd ever sat in. Enoch. Jubilees. Meqabyan. It seemed like a conspiracy. Like something a stranger in a comment section would push on you. But thousands of Christians were describing the same thing in the reviews, and I couldn't shake it. So I bought it. ======== My First Mistake I didn't tell a soul. Not my husband. Not my pastor. Not the women in my Bible study. And I knew exactly why. Because I knew exactly what they'd say. They'd call it fringe. They'd call it a conspiracy. Somebody would say it sounds like a cult, that I was adding books to the Bible, that you can't just go reading whatever you find online and call it scripture. The pastor would give me that careful, concerned look. Half of them would quote me the verse about not adding to the word, the same verse I'd half-worried about myself. So I kept it in a drawer and read it alone, late, after the house was quiet. Like I was getting away with something. That part still bothers me. That a believing woman felt like she had to hide reading more of the word. By the second week, something strange started happening. I read the Book of Enoch first. And the heaviness I'd carried for years, the low dread sitting behind everything, started to loosen. Not all at once. Just a little less every night. I told myself it was a coincidence. ======== The Real Thing Started in Week Three I woke up at three in the morning the way I always did, with that nameless fear pressing down on me. Normally I'd lie there and wait it out for an hour. White-knuckle it until the sun came up. But this time I prayed. And for the first time in longer than I can remember, it didn't feel like the words were bouncing back at me. It felt like they landed. Like I was covered. The dread that had sat on my chest for years. Nothing. It faded before it even took hold, and I rolled over and slept. ======== Here's Where I Almost Made My Biggest Mistake I nearly stopped reading it. I nearly taped that box shut and threw it out. Why? Because that old voice got loud. The one that said this was too much, that real Christians don't go chasing buried books, that I was wandering somewhere I'd regret. So let me say the thing I wish someone had said to me first, because I know it's the exact thing stopping you. This does not replace your King James. I'm not telling you the Bible you grew up with is wrong. I'm not telling you to throw it out. I still read mine every single morning. I didn't trade one Bible for another. This isn't a different Bible. It's the rest of it. It's the twenty-two books that were taken out, handed back to you, sitting next to the sixty-six you already trust. More scripture, not other scripture. The early church read all of it. They didn't see two Bibles. They saw one, whole. Once I understood that, the fear went quiet. I wasn't replacing the word. I was finally reading the parts of it that had been kept from me. Women like us have been conditioned to believe the power the Bible actually talks about was meant for other people. For the apostles, for the saints, for somebody holier than us. That feeling nothing was just the honest Christian life and anything more was suspicious. I almost threw all of it away because feeling that strong felt like a trick. ======== What's Actually Inside These Pages So I finally sat down and studied what was in this Bible that the one I grew up with didn't have. Here's what I found. ✅ The Book of Enoch: the map of the unseen world. The watchers, the fallen ones, the heavens laid out level by level, named and ordered. And here's the part that stopped me cold. The apostle Jude quotes this exact book in the New Testament. "Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied." It's sitting in your King James right now, quoting a book your King James leaves out. ✅ The Book of Jubilees: the history underneath Genesis. The timeline, the watchers' rebellion, the names and the origins that the trimmed version only hints at and never explains. ✅ The Book of the Covenant: the terms the early church understood that most believers today have never read a page of. ✅ The Ascension of Isaiah: the prophet carried up through the heavens, an account that lines up with what Enoch wrote, by a different man, centuries apart. ✅ Meqabyan (1, 2, 3): the Ethiopian books of the Maccabees. The faith-under-siege books, written by the people who actually held the line while empires fell around them. ✅ The prayers, the names of the spirits, and the angels assigned to your own household: the part the early believers used and the rest of the world had taken out of its hands. This wasn't just another Bible with a nicer cover. It was the complete word, the way the early church actually carried it, before sixty-six books got handed out as if that was everything God ever said. ======== And the Book Itself This is the other thing I wasn't expecting. The print is big. Large, clean, easy on the eyes. Not the cramped onionskin micro-text you squint at in most Bibles. You can actually sit and read it for an hour without a headache, and my mother can read it without reaching for her glasses. The translation isn't watered down. Nothing softened to make it more comfortable. Nothing smoothed over to avoid offending anyone. The hard parts are left hard, in plain English you can understand, the way they were actually written. And it's built like something you keep. A real book, a real binding, the kind of thing you hand to your daughter one day, not a flimsy paperback that falls apart in a year. ======== The Side Effect Nobody Warns You About About a month in, my husband said something I haven't stopped thinking about. "You pray different now." I asked him what he meant. He said it used to sound like I was asking permission. Now it sounds like I know who I'm talking to. I hadn't realized how much that quiet dread had been running my life. How much of me had gone silent over the years. How long I'd been a believer who was secretly scared. This Bible didn't just give me more to read. It gave me back something I thought wasn't meant for someone like me. ======== Why Most "Solutions" Make It Worse Before this, I'd tried everything to feel something again. ❌ The cheap Ethiopian Bibles on Amazon. Half the books quietly missing, translations softened past recognition, review after review of believers warning it wasn't the real thing. I almost lost real money on a counterfeit. ❌ Western study guides. They explain around the missing books instead of just handing them to you. A tour of the locked room instead of the key. ❌ Another devotional, another reading plan. More passes through the same sixty-six books, never the twenty-two that were taken out. ❌ Just praying harder. Willpower stacked on top of a Bible with the battle pages torn out of it. None of them touched the root. You were handed sixty-six books and told that was the whole story. The books that explain the unseen world, the ones the apostles were reading, were stripped out before the version you own ever reached your hands. ======== What I Wish Someone Had Told Me Sooner If you're living with: Prayers that feel like they stop at the ceiling and go no further. And please don't make my mistake of almost throwing it out the moment it finally starts working. You deserve to pray and feel it land. You deserve to read the whole story instead of half of it.
